claims.text: The selected high-entropy alloy is produced by arc melting followed by high-temperature homogenization.
The homogenized starting alloy has a largely random elemental distribution.
Extended annealing will promote short-range ordering or nanoscale compositional clustering.
Rapid quenching will preserve a random atomic structure.
Nanoscale compositional ordering reduces lattice distortion.
Nanoscale compositional ordering mitigates electron scattering.
Enhanced local ordering reduces electronic disorder.
Reduced electronic disorder strengthens local electron-phonon coupling.
Stronger electron-phonon coupling facilitates Cooper-pair formation at sufficiently low temperature.
A completely random atomic arrangement disperses scattering channels that hinder pairing.
Annealed samples with short-range ordering will have a higher superconducting critical temperature than quenched, disordered samples.
Alternatively, annealed samples with short-range ordering will have a larger superconducting volume fraction than quenched, disordered samples.
A superconducting transition will be observable as a resistivity drop and onset of diamagnetism.
The proposed ordering effect applies only while processing permits nanoscale reordering without phase separation or secondary-phase formation.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply if processing produces macroscopic segregation.
Intrinsic magnetic contributions from some constituent elements may interfere with superconductivity.
TEM or XRD can verify the intended difference in short-range ordering between annealed and quenched specimens.
A lack of a statistically significant difference in critical temperature or superconducting volume fraction between annealed and quenched samples falsifies the proposed ordering mechanism.
Failure of both annealed and quenched samples to show superconductivity below 20 K falsifies the hypothesis in the stated test regime.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is the as-cast homogenized alloy without an additional ordering treatment, but the predicted comparison and falsification experiment use a rapidly quenched sample as the control. These states are not established as equivalent, so the controlled baseline is inconsistent across fields.
